title: Writing Poetry
description: Composing your own poems — choosing forms, crafting imagery and sound, drafting and redrafting.

notes.heading: Finding Ideas for Poems
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Poem ideas (sometimes called triggers or starting points) are the raw material a poet works from — a memory, an image, a strong feeling, an overheard phrase or an ordinary object seen in a new way.

🔑 How it works
Poems rarely begin with a grand subject; they begin with something small and specific that matters to you. Reliable ways to generate ideas:
• Freewriting — write non-stop for five minutes about anything, then underline the lines that surprise you.
• Mind maps — put one word ("rain", "grandad", "exams") in the centre and branch out every association.
• Lists — "ten things I notice on the way to school" or "five sounds from my kitchen".
• Objects — pick one everyday thing and describe it as if nobody had ever seen it before.
• Strong moments — a first day, an argument, a win, a loss. Specific beats general every time.

💡 Worked Example
Mind map around the word "storm": branches lead to "drumming on the window", "bin lid rolling down the street", "the dog hiding under the table", "lights flickering". Any one of those branches — say, the dog under the table — is already the seed of a poem, because it is a concrete moment rather than an abstract statement like "storms are scary".

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Start from something small, real and specific — not from a big abstract theme.
• Collect ideas constantly; a notebook or phone note of images and overheard lines is a poet's toolkit.
• Freewriting works because you silence the editor in your head until after the ideas exist.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Waiting for a "poetic" subject. A poem about a lost trainer or a burnt piece of toast will usually beat a forced poem about Love or Nature, because you actually have something true to say about it.

notes.heading: Choosing a Form
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A poetic form is a template of rules — about lines, syllables, rhyme or structure — that a poem follows. Choosing a form is one of the first writing decisions you make, and it shapes everything that follows.

🔑 How it works
Match the form to what you want the poem to do:
• Haiku — 3 lines with a 5-7-5 syllable pattern; ideal for capturing one small, sharp moment (traditionally in nature).
• Limerick — 5 lines with an AABBA rhyme scheme and a bouncy rhythm; ideal for jokes and comic characters.
• Sonnet — 14 lines, traditionally in iambic pentameter with a set rhyme scheme; ideal for exploring one big idea or feeling in depth, often with a "turn" near the end.
• Acrostic — the first letters of each line spell a word; a friendly form for beginners.
• Free verse — no fixed rhyme scheme or metre; you make your own rules through line breaks and rhythm. Freedom, but not an excuse for shapelessness.

Rules are not a prison: many poets deliberately bend a form once they know it — but you bend it better when you know what you're bending.

💡 Worked Example
You want to write about the exact second your team scored the winning goal — a single frozen instant. A haiku fits: three short lines force you to catch just the moment. The same event as a story of the whole match would suit free verse or a ballad instead, because those forms have room to move through time.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Every form has rules: haiku 5-7-5, limerick AABBA, sonnet 14 lines — learn them before you break them.
• Choose the form after you know your subject and the effect you want, not before.
• Free verse is a real choice, not the absence of one: you still control line length, breaks and rhythm.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forcing a subject into a form that fights it — squeezing a long, winding story into a haiku, or writing a serious elegy as a limerick whose comic bounce undercuts the mood.

notes.heading: Writing a First Draft
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A draft is an early version of a piece of writing that you expect to change. A first draft is not a failed final poem — it is the raw material the final poem will be built from.

🔑 How it works
1. Write fast. Get the whole poem down without stopping to polish individual words.
2. Don't delete — if a line feels wrong, keep it and write the alternative underneath.
3. Follow surprises: if the poem starts heading somewhere you didn't plan, let it.
4. Stop when the idea is on the page, not when the language is perfect.

The key habit is separating the two jobs: creating (first draft) and judging (redrafting). Trying to do both at once is why most people stall after two lines.

💡 Worked Example
First draft of a line about a crowded bus: "The bus was very full and hot and I couldn't move." Weak — but that's fine. It exists now. In the next draft you can compress it: "shoulders pressed like books on a shelf". You could never have improved the line if you'd refused to write the bad version first.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• A first draft's only job is to exist — quality comes later.
• Write the whole poem before you fix any part of it.
• Keep your crossed-out versions; they often contain the phrase you'll want back.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Editing while drafting. Polishing line one for twenty minutes means line ten never gets written — and that polished line one will probably change anyway once the rest of the poem exists.

✅ Check
Read your first draft and ask only one question: "Is the whole idea on the page?" If yes, the draft has done its job, however rough the wording is.

notes.heading: Crafting Imagery
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Imagery is language that appeals to the senses — sight, sound, smell, touch and taste — so the reader experiences the poem instead of just being told about it. As a writer, imagery is a deliberate choice: you decide which sense to fire and how specific to be.

🔑 How it works
• Show, don't tell: instead of naming a feeling ("I was nervous"), give the reader the physical detail ("my pen tapped the desk and wouldn't stop").
• Be specific: "a magpie" beats "a bird"; "scuffed red trainers" beats "shoes".
• Use more than sight: the smell of cut grass or the grit of sand in a shoe often triggers a stronger memory than a visual.
• Choose comparisons on purpose: a simile ("quiet as snow") or metaphor ("the classroom was a furnace") should match your mood, not just decorate the line.

💡 Worked Example
Telling: "The chip shop was busy and smelled nice."
Showing: "Vinegar stung the air; the queue shuffled forward one cold tile at a time."
The second version never says "busy" or "nice" — the reader concludes both from the sensory evidence. That's imagery doing the work.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Replace statements of feeling with physical details that create the feeling.
• One precise, surprising image beats three vague ones.
• Similes and metaphors are choices: pick comparisons that fit the poem's mood.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Stacking adjectives instead of building an image. "The big, dark, scary, horrible forest" tells the reader what to think; "the path narrowed until the trees knitted overhead" makes them feel it.

notes.heading: Choosing Sounds and Rhymes
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Sound choices are the decisions a poet makes about how a poem lands in the ear: which words rhyme (and how exactly), and which consonant and vowel sounds repeat. Rhyme is a tool with settings, not an on/off switch.

🔑 How it works
Types of rhyme you can choose between:
• Perfect (full) rhyme — the sounds match exactly: hill/thrill, fountain/mountain. Feels satisfying, song-like, sometimes sing-song.
• Half rhyme (imperfect/slant rhyme) — the sounds almost match: daughter/otter, room/storm. Feels unsettled or subtle — useful when perfect rhyme would feel too neat.
• End rhyme — rhyme at the ends of lines; the most common placement.
• Internal rhyme — rhyme inside a single line ("watch me rhyme in the middle of the line"); speeds the line up and adds a playful or rapping energy.

Beyond rhyme, individual sounds carry effects:
• Plosives (p, b, t, d, hard c/g) burst out of the mouth — forceful, angry or emphatic.
• Sibilance (s, soft c) hisses — soothing or sinister depending on context.
• Assonance (repeated vowel sounds) glues a line together musically.

💡 Worked Example
Writing about a playground argument, you might load a line with plosives — "Don't poke, don't push, don't start" — because the hard b/p/t sounds physically feel like jabs. For a lullaby-style poem about the sea you'd do the opposite: soft s and l sounds, "the slow swell slides to shore".

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Choose your rhyme type for effect: perfect rhyme resolves, half rhyme unsettles.
• Never twist the meaning of a sentence just to land a rhyme — if the rhyme forces a word you'd never otherwise use, change the rhyme.
• Read every draft aloud: sound choices can only be judged by ear.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Rhyming for rhyme's sake — ending a line with "blue" and then inventing a random shoe that has nothing to do with the poem, just to complete the pair. The reader always notices the padding.

notes.heading: Line Breaks and Enjambment
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A line break is the point where you end one line and start the next. Because poems don't run to the margin like prose, every break is a decision. Enjambment is the choice to let a sentence run over the break without punctuation, so the reader is pulled into the next line.

🔑 How it works
• A break is a tiny pause. End a line and the reader lingers a split-second on its last word — so put words you want stressed at the ends of lines.
• Enjambment creates speed, flow or suspense: the unfinished sentence drags the eye downwards.
• An end-stopped line (punctuation at the break) creates a full stop in the reading voice — calm, definite, final.
• You can break a line to create a double meaning: the line reads one way alone, then the next line twists it.
• Stanza breaks work the same way at a larger scale — use them to mark a change of time, place, speaker or mood.

💡 Worked Example
Compare two ways of breaking the same sentence:

"I kept every promise / I ever made / except one"

Breaking after "promise" lets the reader believe, for one beat, that the speaker kept them all — then the last line lands the twist. In prose ("I kept every promise I ever made except one") that beat of suspense doesn't exist. The line break did the work.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Line breaks control pace and emphasis: end words get extra weight.
• Enjambment = momentum and surprise; end-stopping = control and finality. Choose per line.
• Try breaking the same draft three different ways and read each aloud — the poem can change completely.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Breaking lines wherever the page happens to run out, or purely to make the poem "look poem-shaped". If a break doesn't change the pace, emphasis or meaning, it's decoration, not craft.

notes.heading: Redrafting, Editing and Sharing
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Redrafting is rewriting a poem — changing words, lines, order and structure — to move it closer to the effect you want. Editing is the final tidy-up: spelling, punctuation and layout. Professional poets treat redrafting as the main event of writing, not an optional extra.

🔑 How it works
• Change one thing at a time and save each version, so you can go back.
• Test single words: swap a weak word for a stronger one and read the line aloud to hear the difference.
• Interrogate your opening and title most of all — they carry the most weight.
• Cut ruthlessly: any line that doesn't add image, sound or meaning is a candidate for deletion.
• Get a response: read the poem to someone, or perform it, and watch where they lean in or drift off.

💡 Worked Example
The First World War poet Wilfred Owen redrafted obsessively, and his manuscripts survive. His famous title "Anthem for Doomed Youth" began as "Anthem for Dead Youth" — one word changed, but "doomed" adds the sense that the soldiers were trapped from the start, and its long vowel even booms like the guns. In another poem he tried "gargling", "gurgling" and "goggling" before settling on "guttering" — the word that best caught the sound of a choking soldier. One word at a time: that's redrafting.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Redrafting means real rewriting — new words, new lines, new order — not just fixing commas.
• Read aloud after every change; the ear catches what the eye misses.
• Titles and first lines deserve the most passes — they decide whether anyone reads the rest.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Calling a spelling check a "redraft". Correcting "teh" to "the" is proofreading; redrafting is asking whether the line, the image and the word order are the strongest you can make them.

✅ Check
Before you call a poem finished: (1) read it aloud, (2) underline the single weakest line and rewrite it once, (3) ask whether the title earns its place. If all three pass, share it — performance and feedback are part of the craft, from class readings to poetry slams, where pace, volume and clarity carry the poem.

flashcards.definition: The first complete version of a poem, written quickly and freely, which you fully expect to change later.
flashcards.example: Getting the whole bus poem down in five rough minutes before improving any single line.

flashcards.definition: Rewriting a poem — swapping words, moving lines, cutting and reordering — to strengthen its effect.
flashcards.example: Wilfred Owen changing his title from 'Anthem for Dead Youth' to 'Anthem for Doomed Youth'.

flashcards.definition: A three-line poem with a 5-7-5 syllable pattern, used to capture one small, sharp moment.
flashcards.example: Traditionally about nature: five syllables, then seven, then five.

flashcards.definition: A five-line comic poem with an AABBA rhyme scheme and a bouncing rhythm.
flashcards.example: Lines 1, 2 and 5 rhyme with each other; the shorter lines 3 and 4 rhyme with each other.

flashcards.definition: A 14-line poem, traditionally in iambic pentameter, suited to exploring one idea or feeling in depth, often with a turn near the end.
flashcards.example: Shakespeare's sonnets develop an argument across three quatrains and turn at the closing couplet.

flashcards.definition: Poetry with no fixed rhyme scheme or metre, where the writer creates shape through line breaks and rhythm.
flashcards.example: Choosing short jagged lines for a panic-filled poem about a fire drill.

flashcards.definition: Rhyme where the sounds match exactly, giving a satisfying, song-like effect.
Rhyme where the sounds only partly match, creating a subtler or more unsettled effect than perfect rhyme.
flashcards.example: Daughter/otter or room/storm — close, but not exact.

flashcards.definition: Rhyme placed inside a single line rather than at its end, adding speed and playful energy.
flashcards.example: Watch me rhyme in the middle of the line.

flashcards.definition: Hard consonant sounds made by forcing air out of the mouth (p, b, t, d, hard c/g), used for force or emphasis.
flashcards.example: Don't poke, don't push, don't start — the p, t and d sounds feel like jabs.

flashcards.definition: Letting a sentence run over a line break without punctuation, pulling the reader quickly into the next line.
flashcards.example: Breaking after 'I kept every promise' so the final line 'except one' lands as a surprise.

flashcards.definition: Poetry written to be performed aloud — as at a poetry slam — where voice, pace, volume and gesture carry the meaning.
flashcards.example: Delivering your key line almost in a whisper so the audience leans in to hear it.

questions.stem: Which is the most reliable way to find an idea for a poem?
choices: Wait until a big, poetic subject like Love or Death occurs to you
Start from a small, specific moment, object or memory that matters to you
Copy the subject of a famous poem you have studied
Choose a rhyme scheme first and let it decide the subject
questions.explanation: Poems grow best from concrete, personal material — a burnt toast, a lost trainer, an overheard line — because you have something true to say about it. Abstract themes usually produce vague poems.

choices: Writing a poem with no rhyme scheme
Writing non-stop for a set time without judging, to generate raw ideas
Publishing your work without charging for it
Writing the final version of a poem in one attempt
questions.explanation: Freewriting means writing continuously for a few minutes with your inner editor switched off, then mining the result for surprising lines. It describes a way of generating ideas, not a verse form.

questions.stem: What is the syllable pattern of a haiku?
choices: 14 lines of 10 syllables
questions.explanation: A haiku has three lines of five, seven and five syllables. Ten-syllable lines over fourteen lines describes a sonnet in iambic pentameter, not a haiku.

questions.stem: Which rhyme scheme does a limerick use?
choices: ABAB
AABBA
ABBA
No rhyme at all
questions.explanation: A limerick has five lines with an AABBA scheme: the first, second and fifth lines rhyme, and the shorter third and fourth lines rhyme with each other.

questions.stem: You want to capture one single, frozen instant — the second a winning goal is scored. Which form fits best?
choices: A sonnet, because it has the most lines
A limerick, because the moment is exciting
A haiku, because its three short lines suit one small, sharp moment
A ballad, because it can tell the story of the whole match
questions.explanation: A haiku's tight 5-7-5 frame forces you to catch just the instant. A ballad would suit the story of the whole match, but the question asks about one frozen second.

questions.stem: What is the main job of a first draft?
choices: To have perfect spelling and punctuation
To get the whole idea onto the page so it can be improved later
To be short enough to fit on one page
To impress the first person who reads it
questions.explanation: A first draft's only job is to exist — quality comes from redrafting afterwards. Judging the language while drafting is what makes writers stall.

questions.stem: Why do writers separate drafting from editing?
choices: Because editing is not allowed until a teacher checks the work
Because trying to create and judge at the same time stalls the writing
Because drafts are never actually changed
Because editing only means fixing spelling
questions.explanation: Creating and judging are different jobs. Polishing line one for twenty minutes while drafting usually means the rest of the poem never gets written.

questions.stem: Which line shows a feeling through imagery instead of telling it?
choices: I was extremely nervous before the exam.
The exam was very scary and difficult.
My pen tapped the desk and wouldn't stop.
I felt quite anxious about the whole situation.
questions.explanation: The tapping pen is a physical detail that lets the reader feel the nervousness rather than being told about it. The other options all name the feeling directly.

questions.stem: Which image is the most specific?
choices: A bird sat in a tree
A creature was outside somewhere
A nice bird sat in a nice tree
A magpie tilted its head on the bare branch
questions.explanation: Naming the species (magpie), the action (tilted its head) and the detail (bare branch) gives the reader a precise picture. 'Nice' and 'somewhere' add no visual information.

choices: A rhyme where the sounds match exactly
A rhyme that only appears in the second half of a poem
A rhyme where the sounds only partly match, like daughter/otter
A rhyme written inside a line instead of at the end
questions.explanation: Half rhyme (also called slant or imperfect rhyme) pairs words that almost rhyme, giving a subtler, unsettled effect. Rhyme inside a line is internal rhyme — a different technique.

questions.stem: Why might a poet load a line about an argument with plosive sounds (p, b, t, d)?
choices: Because plosives make the line longer
Because the hard, bursting sounds feel forceful, like verbal jabs
Because plosives are the only sounds that rhyme
Because plosives make the poem easier to spell
questions.explanation: Plosives are made by forcing air out of the mouth, so they sound punchy and aggressive — the sound reinforces the conflict. Sound choices are judged by ear, not by length or spelling.

questions.stem: What is the danger of rhyming 'for rhyme's sake'?
choices: Rhyme is against the rules of modern poetry
Perfect rhymes are always wrong in serious poems
Rhyming too much makes the poem impossible to perform
You twist in words you'd never otherwise use, and readers notice the padding
questions.explanation: If landing a rhyme forces an unnatural or irrelevant word into the poem, meaning suffers — the fix is to change the rhyme, not the meaning. Rhyme itself is a legitimate tool with settings, not a ban.

questions.stem: Breaking the line after 'I kept every promise' so the poem ends 'except one' on its own line is an example of:
choices: Enjambment used to create a beat of suspense before the twist
An end-stopped line used for finality
A caesura placed by a rhyme scheme
A stanza break marking a new speaker
questions.explanation: The sentence runs over the break without punctuation, so the reader briefly believes every promise was kept — then the final line overturns it. That pull into the next line is enjambment.

questions.stem: Why did Wilfred Owen's change of title from 'Anthem for Dead Youth' to 'Anthem for Doomed Youth' strengthen the poem?
choices: 'Doomed' is easier to spell than 'dead'
'Doomed' has fewer syllables, so the line scans better
'Doomed' suggests the soldiers were trapped from the start, and its booming vowel echoes the guns
The change was required by his publisher
questions.explanation: The single-word swap added meaning (no escape from the start) and sound (a vowel that booms like artillery) — a model of how redrafting one word can transform a poem.

questions.stem: Which of these counts as genuine redrafting rather than proofreading?
choices: Correcting 'teh' to 'the' throughout the poem
Adding full stops to the ends of sentences
Cutting a weak middle stanza and moving the strongest image to the opening line
Changing the font so the poem is easier to read
questions.explanation: Redrafting means rethinking content and structure — cutting, moving and rewriting for effect. Fixing typos, punctuation and formatting is proofreading, which comes after the rewriting is done.
